extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, art historians, and readers of art criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging grotesque ornamentation and its moral/aesthetic qualities in architecture, sculpture, and pictorial art; distinguishes noble vs. base grotesque and explains sources (satire, apathy, uncontrolled imagination, symbolism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentation should be rational and meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: As ignorance and rudeness diminish, ornamentation must become rational, and the grotesqueness disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The noblest lessons may be taught in ornamentation and the most solemn truths compressed into it (example: Book of Genesis bound within leaf-borders of the gates of Ghiberti). By contrast, ornament without meaning ('Raphael's arabesque') is 'mere elaborate idleness' and 'an unnatural and monstrous abortion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Paths by which grotesque rises into higher art
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque may be elevated either by expanding/softening into beauty as skill increases, or by rising into nobler terribleness/sublime when the artist inclines to gloomy contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two modes are exemplified: (1) the craftsman devotes himself to beauty so grotesqueness softens (Ghiberti), (2) the workman’s imperfection or apathy rises into a noble terribleness (Albert Dürer’s grotesque, e.g., Adam and Eve where head of Adam attains true sublime). Use these trajectories to judge whether grotesque attains higher art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mockery / satire in grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and humor in the grotesque can be refreshing and become a principal feature of popular ornament; used rightly, satire serves to show folly and vice as contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where lower orders are allowed free expression, humor/satire enter their work and can be permanently expressed in sculptures (cathedral work). Such satire was historically thought appropriate and useful to make wickedness appear contemptible; when properly applied it 'became permanently expressed in the sculptures of the cathedral.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of evil must show degradation to be convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: To express intense wickedness it is not possible to retain noble or angelic forms; vice requires a degree of corporeal degradation in depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's Satan is criticized as 'too noble' and therefore artistically false; Dante and Bunyan succeed by degrading forms to match wickedness. Full portraiture of excessive vice involves indecency and baseness of thought/act, which in older works could be more frankly depicted (e.g., Inferno books 21–22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for noble vs base satirical grotesque: presence of beauty/dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The noble grotesque is employed by the master for good purposes and to contrast with beauty; the base grotesque lacks mingled forms of beauty or dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple distinguishing test is to observe whether any forms of beauty or dignity are mingled with the grotesque; if none appear, it likely belongs to the base school. Noble grotesque contrasts with and enhances beauty; base grotesque never does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Horror (genuine fear) vs mere disgust
rubrics_metrics.description: Noble grotesque contains authentic horror or fear of sin; base grotesque lacks genuine horror and only provokes disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The base soul has no fear of sin and thus cannot produce genuineness of fear in art; its attempt at terror results merely in disgusting effects. Absence of true horror indicates ignoble grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Nature (accurate rendering of animal character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noble grotesque makes admirable use of animal features—borrowing the expressions of brute creation to indicate vices while retaining power and nobleness; base grotesque shows vulgar exaggeration and false, monstrous forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providence provided animal forms so human vices might be expressed without disgust; a right-minded workman studies these subtle lines. Ignoble workmen are too dull or idle to execute such subtlety and resort to blunt exaggeration, making the work false and monstrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Mercy (pity or sorrow mixed with satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noble satirical grotesque fixes upon human nature with sorrow and infinite tenderness—acknowledging redeeming features; base grotesque has no pity and exists to slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In highest forms, satire retains a compassion (compare the fool in Lear); even bitter sarcasm does not wholly lose sight of the better nature of its target. Absence of mercy is a hallmark of ignoble grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ungovernableness of imagination as a source of grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque may arise from error and wildness of mental impressions—dream-like distortions produced by fear or failure of human faculties to grasp highest truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grotesque of disturbed dreams is the clearest example (imagination deprived of reason). Noble imagination can also be partly ungovernable and prophetic: when whole man is trained, vision may be 'seen as in a perfect mirror' (sublime); when imperfect, the mirror is broken and images are distorted into grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of inspiration (genius) and labor (art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the supremacy of genius and the necessity of labor are required: imagination/gift is essential and cannot be fully replaced by study and toil; yet art and training matter too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against attempts (e.g., some German school) to substitute learned, laborious methods for the painting faculty; forced, over-intellectualized work lacks healthy practice of a strong artist. The truly great man humbled by Revelations contrasts with the conceit of the weak who mistake learned conceits for greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distortion vs dimness: degree of grotesque proportional to narrowed grasp
rubrics_metrics.description: If truth is seen in wholeness and quiet, the vision is sublime; if narrowed and broken by human capacity, it becomes grotesque—the more the dimming/breaking, the greater the grotesqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy of mirror: a dim mirror (dulness) shows truth darkly; a broken/distorted mirror creates grotesque images. Many biblical visions and prophetic imagery are grotesque because they are narrowed symbolic intimations of great truths (e.g., Jacob's ladder, Joseph's dreams, Ezekiel's beasts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolical grotesque: use of uncouth symbols to evoke awe
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic or grotesque forms—even uncouth, ludicrous, or mean external shapes—are acceptable when they veil deeper, awe-inspiring truth and thereby increase solemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols (e.g., the four living creatures for the Evangelists) were preferred because they conveyed that invisible greatness beyond human form; their apparent insignificance or uncouthness enhanced mystery and piety. Designers sometimes exploited this by overlaying impurity with sacred interpretation, but the potency of symbol rests on conveying deeper meaning rather than external beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque born of terror and contemplation of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the most sublime grotesques arise from terror and the human contemplation of death—leading to images softened by sorrow and capable of ennobling thought about the eternal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The charnel-house and skeleton imagery furnish terrible grotesque related to the human frame; northern images (kelpie, wraith, phantoms, ghosts) developed from fear of death and combine degradation (paralyzing terror) with ennobling thoughts of eternity. This source can produce sublime—and not merely ignoble—grotesque when tempered by affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of noble grotesque as a test of cultural/individual greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of a noble grotesque indicates a healthy, vigorous balance of imagination, emotion, and intellect in a period, nation, or individual; absence indicates comparative smallness or limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where human mind is healthy and not overborne by mere reasoning, grotesque exists in full energy. Dante, Michael Angelo, Tintoret, and Shakespeare are exemplars where the grotesque attains noble development; lack of grotesque invention suggests cultural limitation.
